title: Reading Big Words: What It Looks Like in the Classroom, the School, and the State
author: Secondary Literacy Commons
summary: This Secondary Literacy Commons roundup brings together three practitioners working at different system scales -- a classroom interventionist in rural Wyoming, a science teacher developing a whole-school model, and a state ELA specialist in Arizona -- all focused on helping secondary students read morphologically complex and multisyllabic words. Wyoming interventionist Faith Howard emphasizes the reciprocal relationship between encoding and decoding: students who spell and write words build stronger orthographic maps than those who only read them. The piece shows how the same challenge -- decoding 'big words' -- looks different depending on whether you work one-on-one, build school-wide systems, or set state policy. Cross-scale coherence matters: classroom expertise must be supported by coordinated structures to have wide impact, and isolated good practice disappears when individual practitioners move on.
points: * Decoding 'big words' at the secondary level requires explicit morphological instruction: breaking words into prefixes, roots, and suffixes gives students productive strategies for unfamiliar vocabulary. * The reciprocal relationship between encoding and decoding is central: students who write and spell words build stronger orthographic maps than those who only read them. * Effective word instruction is anchored in the texts students are currently reading -- not isolated vocabulary lists -- ensuring learned words are immediately usable for comprehension. * Cross-scale coherence matters: classroom interventionists, school literacy leaders, and state specialists need aligned frameworks to prevent islands of good practice from disappearing. * Secondary students rarely receive explicit decoding instruction because the assumption is that decoding is finished by middle school -- a systemic gap that disproportionately affects students with learning disabilities and ELL students.
quotes: It was a coherent picture of what this work looks like when it's done with intention, at every level of the system.
From the Classroom: Faith Howard, Wyoming Faith Howard is a 6-12 literacy interventionist and specialist in rural Wyoming, with a background as a high school English teacher.
Her message was simple and urgent: decoding alone is only half the equation.

Faith has built her intervention work around the reciprocal relationship between encoding and decoding -- the idea that orthographic mapping doesn't fully happen unless students are also learning to spell and write the words they're learning to read.

She pulls directly from the texts her students are reading that week -- novels like Just Mercy or The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks -- choosing words that are tier two or tier three, morphologically rich, and essential for comprehending, discussing, and writing about the text.

She cross-references those words against a diagnostic spelling screener to identify patterns where her students are struggling, then groups the words accordingly to double-dip on both pronunciation and spelling instruction.
On Mondays, students work through word pyramids -- isolating each syllable of a word, building up slowly, with bonus questions about vowel variability.
